Cleveland, Ohio. Franklin Castle, 4308 Franklin Boulevard, built 1881 to 1883.

In Cleveland's Ohio City neighborhood stands a rock-faced sandstone mansion with a round corner tower, four stories, more than twenty rooms and eighty windows. German immigrant Hannes Tiedemann, a wholesale grocer who became a banker, built it from 1881 to 1883, back when Franklin Boulevard was one of the most upscale streets in the city. Today most Clevelanders know it as Franklin Castle, and it's often called the most haunted house in Ohio.

The legend grows out of the Tiedemann family's grief. Their daughter Emma died of diabetes in 1881 at age 15, and the stories say her ghost and her mother Louise's still wander the house. Around the time a German singing club sold the building in 1968, those rumors spread across Cleveland's west side. The family who lived there from 1968 to 1974 claimed the house was haunted, and one of them said she was warned the house was evil and that she should move out. After they left in 1974, the next owner offered public tours of "haunted" Franklin Castle. In 1975, a reporter was photographed exploring a hidden room behind a panel, and human bones turned up in a closet that same year.

Now the debate. Cleveland Historical points out that Emma died before the house was even finished, and that despite the rumors circulating since the 1960s, none of the Tiedemann children died in it. Like many families of that era, the Tiedemanns had lost three infant children to disease between 1863 and 1873, long before this house existed. The Encyclopedia of Cleveland History calls the haunted house stories spurious and says they don't seem to go back before 1965. And those bones? They're believed to have been planted by the owner to drum up publicity for his ghost tours. The rumored secret passages for Prohibition bootlegging don't exist either, apart from a small servants' stairway.

The house has had a rough run since. Michael DeVinko, Judy Garland's last husband, restored it and lived there for over a decade. Shortly after he sold it in 1999, an arsonist set it on fire, and in 2011 new owners bought it and kept restoring. Ghost hunters still come knocking, including Ghost Adventures in 2020. So is Franklin Castle haunted, or just a beautiful old house that got a reputation?

Source: https://clevelandhistorical.org/items/show/531

Birmingham, Alabama. Sloss Furnaces, 1882 to 1971.

For almost ninety years, the towering blast furnaces at Sloss turned out pig iron in the heart of Birmingham. The first blast was in April 1882, and the furnaces didn't go cold until 1971. Instead of letting it be torn down, Birmingham voters approved a $3.3 million bond in 1977 to save it, and in 1981 it became a National Historic Landmark, the only blast furnace in the country preserved and restored for public use.

Its best known ghost story actually started across town. On September 10, 1887, Theophilus Calvin Jowers, an assistant foundryman at Alice Furnace, was working around the edge of the furnace to loosen a bell when he lost his balance and fell with it into the molten iron. According to Alabama storyteller Kathryn Tucker Windham, he had once promised his wife, Sarah, "as long as there's a furnace standing in this county, I'll be there."

Later stories say workers soon saw him making his rounds, checking on his old crew. Others reported a male figure moving through spots far too hot for anyone to survive, or a sudden cold. When the first Alice Furnace came down in 1905, his ghost was said to turn up at a second furnace until it closed in 1927, and then to move across town to Sloss. In Windham's telling, his son John said he saw a ghostly figure striding through the hot furnace at Sloss from the 1st Avenue North Viaduct in 1927.

Here's where the debate comes in. Look up Sloss ghosts today and the name you'll see most is James "Slag" Wormwood, a brutal graveyard shift boss said to have fallen into the furnace in October 1906 and to haunt the place ever since. But according to Bhamwiki, Birmingham's local history wiki, Slag is a fictional creation, invented by the marketers of the Sloss Fright Furnace haunted attraction, which ran every October from 1998 to 2019. In 2022 the Sloss board decided the event didn't fit the landmark's mission, and it never came back.

So the real story may be stranger than the marketing: a ghost legend that seems to start with a real 1887 death, with a made-up villain stacked on top of it decades later. Is anyone still working the night shift at Sloss?

For more than a century, people in the mountains of western North Carolina have pulled over at dark overlooks and waited for the Brown Mountain lights to appear.

Top 5 things to know about the Brown Mountain lights:

1) The Brown Mountain lights are reported ghost lights near Brown Mountain in North Carolina, watched from spots like the Brown Mountain Overlook on NC Highway 181 near Jonas Ridge, North Carolina, Wiseman's View and Table Rock in the Linville Gorge Wilderness, and overlooks on the Blue Ridge Parkway.

2) The earliest published mentions date from around 1910 to 1912. A September 24, 1913 report in the Charlotte Daily Observer described red "mysterious lights seen just above the horizon every night," showing up "punctually" at 7:30 PM and again at 10 PM.

3) Locals asked their Congressmen for an investigation. In 1913, USGS employee D.B. Sterrett concluded the lights were Southern Railway locomotive headlights, and in 1922 USGS scientist George R. Mansfield used a map and an alidade telescope to show that the lights people were seeing were trains, car headlights and brush fires.

4) The legend kept growing anyway. A ghost story about a murdered woman and baby took in the lights in 1936, a claim of Native American lore first showed up in print in 1938 with no sources, and Scotty Wiseman's 1961 song "The Legend of the Brown Mountain Lights" made them the most popular ghost story in North Carolina.

5) Today they still draw ghost hunters and, since 2022, an annual Brown Mountain Lights Festival in Morganton. But low light cameras installed by Appalachian State University had logged 6,300 viewing hours by 2014 without recording a single unexplainable light.

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brown_Mountain_lights

In July 1952, radar operators watched unknown blips swarm over the White House and the Capitol in Washington, D.C., and fighter jets were sent up to chase them.

Top 5 things to know about the 1952 Washington, D.C. UFO flap:

1) From July 12 to 29, 1952, a wave of UFO sightings hit Washington, D.C., with the biggest nights on back-to-back weekends, July 19 to 20 and July 26 to 27. It became known as the Washington flap, the Washington National Airport Sightings, or the Invasion of Washington.

2) At 11:40 p.m. on July 19, air traffic controller Edward Nugent at Washington National Airport spotted seven objects on his radar, and senior controller Harry Barnes later wrote that "their movements were completely radical compared to those of ordinary aircraft." When objects moved over the White House and the Capitol, Barnes called Andrews Air Force Base, where an airman in the tower saw what looked like "an orange ball of fire, trailing a tail."

3) On July 26 the blips came back, and F-94 Starfire jets were scrambled from New Castle Air Force Base in Delaware. Lieutenant William Patterson chased four white glows, and according to Project Blue Book spokesman Albert Chop, he radioed, "I see them now and they're all around me. What should I do?" Nobody answered, Chop said, because nobody knew what to tell him.

4) Headlines like "SAUCERS SWARM OVER CAPITAL" ran across the country, President Harry Truman had his air force aide call Blue Book chief Edward J. Ruppelt for an explanation, and the Pentagon press conference on July 29 was the largest since World War II.

5) The Air Force blamed temperature inversions for the radar blips and misidentified stars, meteors and city lights for the visual sightings. Not everyone bought it. Former controller Howard Cocklin told the Washington Post in 2002, "I saw it on the [radar] screen and out the window."

In the summer of 1978, something big, hairy and walking on two legs kept coming back to one family's backyard outside Minerva, Ohio.

Top 5 things to know about the Minerva Monster:

1) The Minerva Monster is the name given to a Bigfoot-like creature reported in August 1978 along U.S. Route 30, just west of Minerva, Ohio, in Paris Township, Stark County, behind the Cayton family home, where an old abandoned strip mine gave way to dense woods.

2) It started earlier that month, when the Caytons' grandchildren ran into the house crying that they had seen a large hairy monster in the pit. The adults who went out to look described a creature covered in dark matted hair, about 7 feet tall and 300 pounds, with no visible neck. "It just stood there," Evelyn Cayton said.

3) On the night of August 21, family and friends on the front porch saw two pairs of yellow eyes by an old chicken coop. Headlights showed two cougar-like cats, and then a large hairy figure on two legs stepped in front of them as if to protect them. Minutes later it stood at the kitchen window, about four yards from the table, for close to ten minutes before it left.

4) Stark County Deputy Sheriff James Shannon arrived about five minutes after it was gone and said the lingering stench smelled like "ammonia-sulphur." Deputies searched the area on horseback and in jeeps and turned up only unusual but unsubstantiated footprints, and more sightings followed on August 22 and 23 and into September.

5) The bear explanation never settled it. The Ohio Division of Wildlife dismissed bears at the time, investigators said local law enforcement leaned on the bear story partly to keep vigilantes and hunters out of the woods, and when asked if she had seen bears, Evelyn Cayton answered, "No, not unless they were mutated."

Occoquan, Virginia. Reported October 19, 2026.

Thirteen years ago, the ghost of a little boy was reported at Puzzle Palooza, a puzzle shop at 408 Mill St. in Occoquan. There were flickering lights, doors opening on their own, and puzzles that were mysteriously solved, with their boxes rearranged. The puzzle shop is gone now. Some people insist the boy is not.

Local artist and psychic Rachael Bright bought the business in 2019 and opened her art gallery, Local Colour. She told InsideNoVa that the day after she moved in, she found one of her painting smocks stretched out across the doorway. The smocks were the last thing off the moving truck, and she had set them down and forgotten about them. The door was locked and alarmed, and when she asked the landlord, he couldn't explain it either. "Somehow it unpacked itself and ... stretched itself across the welcome mat," she said.

Bright says she has since seen and spoken to the ghost, a 7-year-old boy named Tad Loef. She says he told her he had a Dutch family and two younger siblings, and that his father came over from the Netherlands around World War II. Local records have not been able to confirm his story, but Bright believes him. She now runs ghost tours in town and keeps them age-appropriate for Tad.

He isn't the only one, she says. A Civil War soldier is said to keep walking up the stairs at the metaphysical shop 13 Magical Moons, and another spirit in the oldest house in Occoquan tells visitors about the town's divisions during the Civil War. Local baker Cindy Najera says Tad once asked her if she was a baker, and she still brings him sugar cookies at least once every two months.

None of it can be proven, and the main witness is a psychic medium who says she lives with doubt from others. But in a small town where shop owners leave cookies for a ghost, the story of Tad isn't going anywhere.

Bar Harbor, Maine. Saturday, October 3, 2026, 9:15 p.m.

A couple from Westbrook had driven up for a weekend at the KOA campground in Bar Harbor, just over the bridge from Trenton and Ellsworth. They love to camp and stargaze, and that night they were sitting by the water in complete darkness, looking at a crystal-clear Milky Way with not a cloud in the sky.

According to the report filed with the National UFO Reporting Center, the witness looked north toward the airport and saw what seemed to be a satellite, until it slowed, stopped and darted back the other way. Then both of them noticed a cluster of five or six bright lights making wild maneuvers. The lights didn't blink. They darted back and forth, stopped, and climbed so high they faded out of sight, then came back. Sometimes they came together and hovered close, "almost like they were mingling or interacting with each other," then took off from each other at crazy speeds, in unison.

What unnerved the witness most happened twice. As a commercial plane approached the airport, one of the lights dropped lower and followed it, staying behind it until it was close to landing, then darted back up into the sky. The witness wrote that if these were some kind of military drone, there would be no way they'd be allowed near a commercial plane like that.

They watched for about 25 minutes. "I am not a tinfoil hat type of person," the witness wrote, adding that their partner is extremely levelheaded. They were so bewildered they went back to the cabin, packed their bags and drove home that night.

NUFORC posted it as report 201445 on October 14. Drones and aircraft can't be ruled out from a written report, and the witness lists aircraft nearby. But lights trailing planes on approach are not something you forget.

Juarez Valley, Chihuahua, Mexico, across the Rio Grande from El Paso, Texas. October 2026.

Something is said to be killing chickens, roosters and rabbits in the farm country along the river, and Mexico's best-known UFO investigator says it is not any animal he knows.

Jaime Maussan, who has covered UFOs on Mexican TV for more than three decades, calls it "El Ser de Valle de Juarez," the Juarez Valley Creature. He described it to Juarez outlet NetNoticias.Mx on October 12 as a small, hairless, alien-like being. "It's a predator. I'm not saying it's extraterrestrial, but it is something scary," he said. "It has agility. It has intelligence. It walks on two feet. It appears human. It has a head like a human." According to the El Paso Times, Maussan claimed that witnesses have seen it, including a boy who watched it grab a chicken by the head and scramble up a tree. Maussan says he doesn't believe it would attack people.

His team says a camera trap recorded it in the Juarez Valley on October 14, between 7 and 8 at night, and on October 17 they showed images of a pale white shape climbing over a wall. The descriptions don't line up neatly. Maussan first put it at about 70 centimeters, a little over two feet tall, while his research assistants, measuring against the bricks in the wall, estimated it at almost six feet long with a tail of about three feet. His show has also tied it to dead chickens and the deaths of two horses near Samalayuca.

Maussan has a long history of strange claims, and he compares this one to "El Ser de Metepec," the little creature a farmer near Mexico City said he caught in a trap in 2007. Juarez Civil Protection says it has received no reports of the creature, and police on the U.S. side told the El Paso Times there have been no reports of farm animal deaths or unexplained encounters. So far it's one investigator, a few camera images and a lot of nervous talk in the valley.

Hillyard, Spokane, Washington. Reported October 15, 2026.

In Spokane's historic Hillyard business district stands an old Masonic Temple built in 1931. Upstairs it is the Hill House Event Center, with high ceilings, chandeliers and a vintage ballroom. Downstairs, under the Bison Bar, the basement is a maze of tucked-away rooms full of dusty furniture, old sinks, salvaged fixtures and chandeliers from different decades, plus a room of taxidermy heads with an entire bear standing in the dark.

The owner, Aaron Fiorini, asked the Spokane Paranormal Society to come in after hearing activity while he was alone in the building. On a weekend in September, the group ran an investigation that stretched about 45 hours, from Friday afternoon to Sunday morning, and an Inlander reporter went along.

Co-founder Mark Porter decided to sleep there alone on Friday night. Once everything got quiet, he says, the activity started: voices, footsteps, and something running up and down the stairs in the empty building. On Saturday night the team set up cameras on the balconies and around the ballroom, including a structured light sensor camera that turns what it picks up into stick figures on a screen.

In the basement, the group's psychic medium, Amy Forness, says she spoke with a woman in a formal dress named Jocelyn, still looking for her husband, Lucas. According to Forness, Jocelyn said a group of men in hats took him away one day, and she has not seen him since. Forness called the building a "Grand Central Station in Hillyard" for spirits. Porter says they encountered six spirits there and one negative entity, which Forness described as being "like smoke." Porter, a nondenominational Christian, says the team sometimes asks God to send in the archangel Michael.

The group says it spends a lot of time debunking first. "Not every bump or every scrape is a ghost," Porter said, and an orb on camera could just be dust. As for the spirit work, Porter calls it "highly metaphysical stuff and nothing that we could prove beyond a shadow of a doubt."

Chester, New York. September 26, 2026, about 8:30 p.m.

A driver heading along Craigville Road outside Chester saw three lights off in the distance. Less than a minute later, the road curved and the lights were out of sight.

According to the report the witness filed with the National UFO Reporting Center, it was right after crossing the train tracks that the object showed up again. It came in from the northwest and passed directly over the car, about 200 feet up, moving slowly to the southeast at what the witness guessed was around 30 miles an hour. It was large and gray, about the size of a commercial airliner, and shaped like a triangle, with lights along its sides and bottom and what looked like a circular ring of lights in the center underneath. It made no sound at all.

"I was in shock," the witness wrote, and stopped the car to grab a phone and take a photo. The phone's night setting, which tries to brighten dark pictures, turned the shot into a blur. The craft kept drifting slowly and passed overhead and out behind the car. The whole sighting lasted about three minutes.

The report was filed later that same night, and NUFORC posted it as report 201183 on October 2 along with the witness's photo and a sketch. NUFORC added a note that the last image on the report is an AI reconstruction based on the original photo, the description and the sketch, so it is not a real picture of the craft. It is a single witness, and no one else has come forward publicly. But a silent, airliner-sized triangle 200 feet over a country road is hard to forget.

Portland, Oregon. Old Town, 1880.

In 1880, three successful lumber barons built the Merchant Hotel in what was then called the Old North End, a part of Portland with a rather questionable reputation. Today Old Town Pizza & Brewing sits in the original hotel lobby, and its order window is the old reception desk. Under the floorboards are basements that tours bill as the famous Shanghai tunnels, said to have been used to nab unsuspecting sailors and carry them to ships docked on the Willamette River.

The building also has a resident ghost. Her name is Nina, pronounced "Nigh-na." As the legend goes, she was a young woman sold into prostitution at the hotel. Traveling missionaries convinced her to share information in exchange for freeing her, and soon afterward she was found dead, thrown down the elevator shaft. Staff say she never left. Diners describe a presence behind them or a faint waft of perfume, and Nina is often reported in a black dress, watching people eat and wandering the basement below. Some even wonder if she carved her own name into the brick of the old elevator shaft, which is now the backdrop of a booth in the back.

Historians, though, say the tunnels themselves are the bigger ghost story. The Oregon Historical Society's Oregon Encyclopedia calls it a myth that has grown since the 1970s, with claims of a secret network running under the waterfront, 1,500 or more men abducted every year, and the whole thing hushed up to protect Portland's genteel reputation. Shanghaiing was real. A crimp would hand a drunk or drugged sailor to a ship's captain for a fee often called blood money, and it happened in West Coast ports until steamships ended it around World War I. But historians have found no evidence of any tunnel network built for it.

The tunnel legend seems to trace back to romanticized Sunday Oregonian stories by journalist Stewart Holbrook in 1933, several of dubious authenticity, and to Michael P. Jones, who in the 1970s said he had discovered long-hidden tunnels and started giving tours. The passages that do exist were mostly built to move goods from the docks into basements. As the encyclopedia puts it, "Those who tour the so-called shanghai tunnels today walk into a basement, not through any iniquitous tunnels." So if Nina still walks down there, she may be haunting a legend as much as a hotel.

Source: https://www.oregonencyclopedia.org/articles/shanghai_tunnels_myth/

Lake Lanier, northeast of Atlanta, Georgia. April 1958.

To most Georgians, Lake Lanier is a place for boats and summer weekends. With about 12 million visitors in a single year, it is one of the most visited lakes the Army Corps of Engineers runs anywhere in the nation. But for decades it has also carried a darker reputation. Legend has it the ghost of a long-dead woman roams the lake in a flowing blue dress, mysterious arms reach out for swimmers from the watery depths, and angry spirits call people home to submerged graves.

The most famous tale is the Lady of the Lake. According to the story, a Ford sedan carrying two women careened off a bridge in April 1958 and tumbled into the water, and some say the ghost of one of those women still wanders the bridge at night in a blue dress, lost and restless. Divers have their own stories. In 2017 longtime diver Buck Buchannon told local media, "You reach out into the dark and you feel an arm or a leg and it doesn't move." Others claim to hear church bells ringing from a sunken church far below.

So is the lake cursed? It was created in the 1950s by flooding whole valley communities, and some 700 families sold a total of 56,000 acres to the government. Army Corps of Engineers spokesman Cesar Yabor told CNN the Corps moved the marked graves, but it is likely some unmarked ones were inadvertently left behind. An old auto racing track near Gainesville still sits on the bottom. The church bells, though, he said are not possible, since no such structure was known to be left behind. Georgia's Department of Natural Resources counted 203 deaths in drownings and boating incidents between 1994 and October 2020, and Yabor says the lake's size and popularity feed the tall tales, while its high visitation rate also means more fatalities.

The real history under the water is darker than any ghost story. Part of the lake covers the former town of Oscarville, a small Black community, and in 1912 white mobs drove all 1,098 Black residents out of Forsyth County. Historian Lisa Russell, author of Underwater Ghost Towns of North Georgia, put it this way: "The real haunting in this story is how history has made it impossible to ignore what was done to the land in North Georgia."

On one South Carolina beach, seeing a ghost might be the luckiest thing that ever happens to you.

Top 5 things to know about the Gray Man of Pawleys Island:

1) The Gray Man is a ghost reportedly seen on the coast of Pawleys Island, South Carolina, who warns residents of coming severe storms and hurricanes. Most versions of the legend say he was first seen in 1822, three years before the town government was incorporated.

2) Legend holds that he was a young man traveling from Charleston to see his fiancée in 1822, when he and his horse were caught in the quicksand-like pluff mud of the marshes before Pawleys Island and died. His spirit has haunted the shore nearby ever since, looking for the girl he loved.

3) He has been described as a man wearing gray clothing and a long coat, dressed "like a pirate," and sometimes as having no legs. People who say they encountered him credit him with saving them or their homes from severe storms.

4) He became nationally famous after Hurricane Hugo in 1989, when residents Jim and Clara Moore told Unsolved Mysteries they saw a man on the beach who disappeared when they waved. Their house was spared while their neighbors' homes were heavily damaged.

5) The legend appears to have first entered print in Julian Stevenson Bolick's 1946 book Waccamaw Plantations, The Weather Channel gave him an entire episode of American Super/Natural in 2014, and his last reported sighting came just before Hurricane Florence hit in 2018.

In a single night in 1957, the phones at one small Texas police station would not stop ringing.

Top 5 things to know about the Levelland UFO case:

1) On the night of November 2 and 3, 1957, the police department in Levelland, Texas, a town of about 10,000 west of Lubbock on the flat South Plains, received a total of 15 UFO-related reports, and Officer A. J. Fowler noted that "everybody who called was very excited."

2) The first call came from farm workers Pedro Saucedo and Joe Salaz, who said they saw a blue flash near the road 4 miles west of town, their truck's engine died and a rocket-shaped object rose up and passed over them. "It sounded like thunder and my truck rocked from the flash...I felt a lot of heat," Saucedo said. Fowler thought it was a joke.

3) Then the calls kept coming. Jim Wheeler reported a "brilliantly lit, egg-shaped object" about 200 feet long sitting in the road east of town, Texas Tech student Newell Wright saw a 100-foot-long egg-shaped object in the road, and farmer Frank Williams, Ronald Martin and James Long all said their engines and headlights died until a glowing object flew away.

4) Even the authorities saw something. Sheriff Weir Clem watched a brilliant red object move across the sky at 1:30 AM, and fifteen minutes later Fire Chief Ray Jones also saw an object as his own vehicle's headlights and engine had trouble.

5) Project Blue Book sent a sergeant who spent seven hours in town and blamed ball lightning or St. Elmo's fire, with the stalled cars put down to "wet electrical circuits." But astronomer J. Allen Hynek later wrote that he was "not proud today" that he hastily agreed, noting that "observers reported overcast and mist but no lightning."

Something howls in the Ozark Mountains after dark, and nobody can agree on what it is.

Top 5 things to know about the Ozark Howler:

1) The Ozark Howler is a cryptid of Arkansas folklore, said to roam the Ozark Mountains of northern Arkansas, northeastern Oklahoma and southern Missouri, and one of its best known modern reports comes from a dark road in Springdale, Arkansas.

2) Tradition describes it as bear-like in shape with a dark, shaggy coat, while other versions of the legend describe a cat-like animal with glowing eyes and horns.

3) Its origins may reach back to a late 18th century report by Daniel Boone, who claimed to have killed a large, hairy creature in the region, although most reported sightings come from the 20th century.

4) In October 2014, a motorist called the Arkansas Game and Fish Commission at 9:45 PM after nearly colliding with a bear-sized, gray, fast-running animal on Pump Station Road in Springdale, and call records suggest armed state wildlife officers may have been sent to investigate.

5) In December 2015, a viewer sent 40/29 News photos said to show the Howler on the Yellow Rock Trail at Devils Den. The Game and Fish Commission said it had heard of no sightings and called the images a hoax, and a biologist said the legend ranks right up there with the tales of Bigfoot.

Octagon Hall, Franklin, Kentucky. October 2026.

Some say one of the most haunted buildings in Kentucky is Octagon Hall in Franklin, an eight-sided house with a heavy Civil War history, including time as a field hospital. It hosts ghost hunts now, and the people who spend their nights there told WBKO the stories keep coming.

Paranormal investigator Cameron Hesson says you hear footsteps all night, voices that aren't attached to a body, and doors opening and closing on their own. One encounter still stands out to him. Walking upstairs with a friend, he felt something grab and pull his hair, hard enough that he felt his scalp move. His friend looked at him and said, "Brother, I hate to be the one to tell you this, but you don't have hair."

Director of operations Beth Allen says it has gotten physical with her too. A silver teapot, heavy enough to hurt, was sitting near some knives laid out in view of a camera. The camera wasn't aimed at the teapot itself, but she says you could see it shaking. "It came off, hit a cup, and hit me in the back of the head."

She has seen apparitions as well. Recently, a group was sitting in the dining room when a man walked past the doorway. "We knew we were the only people here in the home, and a man walked by clear as day. We all saw him past the doorway."

The most talked-about spirit is a little girl named Mary. Allen says embers from the fire hit her dress and she was badly burned. Others have reported a woman in white, and figures they believe were former residents of the home. Hesson's theory is that some of them found something they were attached to and didn't want to leave.

Skeptics would point to an old house settling, drafts and the power of suggestion on a ghost hunt, and the camera wasn't pointed at the teapot. Either way, the hall is adding extra ghost hunts for the Halloween season.

Kingsport, Tennessee. October 8, 2026, about 2:15 a.m.

The witness lives in the mountains and likes to look at the night sky early in the morning. Around 2:15 a.m., walking the dogs on a hill at their apartment complex, they looked up and saw something they say was nothing like anything they had seen in their life.

It was a large teardrop-shaped craft, "very dark black like dirty black," and from where they stood it looked about the size of three semi trucks. It moved so slowly it almost seemed to stop. It had a couple of lights on it and a haze around it, and its surface looked like it had water on it, "maybe a transparency." It made a swooshing sound, like the ocean. And it wasn't alone. The witness says it was escorted by four smaller craft.

They watched it for about 20 minutes, high overhead, as it drifted toward Morristown, until they couldn't see it anymore. "I live in the mountains so at 2:15 in the morning I thought this is odd, no planes out."

The report was filed with the National UFO Reporting Center later that same morning and posted October 13. The witness listed a military background. It is a single witness, and NUFORC hasn't attached any explanation. Slow, quiet lights moving in a group have turned out to be aircraft or drones before. But a wet-looking, dirty black teardrop the size of three semis, with an ocean sound and four escorts, is not what anyone expects to see on a 2 a.m. dog walk.

Near Forks, Washington. Thursday, October 15, 2026.

Two strange reports came out of the same corner of the Olympic Peninsula on the same day, about two miles apart, and the Bigfoot Society podcast has been putting them side by side.

The first came from a couple staying at a cabin about nine miles outside Forks, in the Sol Duc River area near Quillayute Airport. She thought they were in Washington for a work trip. He had actually planned a surprise proposal, and she said yes. But sometime between 1 and 2:30 that morning, she found she couldn't move, and she described a voice in her head that wanted her to go outside. She was too scared to go, and tried to wake him by mumbling. When he finally woke up and nudged her, it stopped. He says nothing like it had ever happened to her before. He wrote in asking whether it could be connected to Bigfoot. No creature was seen.

The second report came that same afternoon, around 2:30. According to Tom Sewid of Sasquatch Island, one of his team members was driving toward Forks from the Quillayute Airport area, towing a trailer. As he passed an active gravel pit, he looked out his passenger window and saw a large black figure standing upright beside a white metal entrance gate, about 35 yards off the road. He saw its left side. It seemed to be looking into the gravel pit. He only had a few seconds, and by the time he found a place to turn the trailer around and come back, it was gone.

The witness had a tape measure, so he measured the gate: four feet, two inches from the ground to the top. During the follow-up, Sewid stood by the gate and raised his hand over his head, about 7 feet to 7 feet 2 inches off the ground, and the witness said the figure had been around that tall, possibly taller.

Waking up unable to move is the textbook description of sleep paralysis, and a few seconds' look from a moving truck leaves room for a bear. But two reports on the same day, two miles apart, along the Sol Duc River is the kind of overlap that keeps people watching the tree line out there.

Fort Washakie, Wind River Reservation, Wyoming. Reported October 17, 2026.

For four years, Leslie Shakespeare patrolled the Wind River Reservation as a Bureau of Indian Affairs police officer. He told Cowboy State Daily that not everything he ran into on those shifts was of this world.

The story he tells best started with a bear call one summer. The man who reported the bear said he had first tried to wave over another officer down by the parade grounds near the World War II memorial, an officer whose clothes looked different, with a coat and a small hat. Shakespeare told him nobody else was on duty. Later that night, doing security checks, he saw a man matching that description walk between two buildings. When he drove up, no one was there. Another officer and housing security hadn't seen anyone either.

Then people who worked at the agency told him about the old fort soldier. He wears an old uniform with a wool coat, cap and striped pants, and he walks the grounds "as if it might have been his post," always turning up by the parade grounds. He had always been seen around Building One, the first building put up at Fort Washakie, back when it was still an active military post in the late 1800s.

A fire wrecked Building One in the early 2000s, and in 2023 it was torn down. Shakespeare says that as the walls came down, a storm came out of nowhere and swirled above the building, then went away just as quickly when the last wall fell. "After that, nobody's reported seeing the soldier," he said.

His other stories are just as strange. Three people, including the man he was driving to detention, saw a young passenger riding beside him in his patrol car, but the seat was empty and the dash cam showed no one. At the old Fort Washakie School, a boys' boarding school that had sat abandoned for years, he and another officer heard heavy steps and a giggle in an empty building. He later learned graves had been found on the property. And once, tracking a suspect at five in the morning in the dark, he says a light kept appearing to show him which way to go, until he found the man hiding.

There is no photo of the soldier, and the stories rest on what Shakespeare and the people around him say they saw. Shakespeare says he was never afraid. "I felt like I had someone helping me."

Near the St. Anthony Sand Dunes, Idaho. October 3, 2026, around 10 p.m.

Out past Jenkins Will, about 28 miles northwest of Rexburg, the land opens into the St. Anthony Sand Dunes, a long stretch of pale sand that goes dark and quiet after sundown. One local witness says that is exactly when the lights come out.

According to the report filed with the National UFO Reporting Center, the activity starts at the same time whenever it happens, around 10 p.m., and lasts an hour or two. Many white orbs show up in the sky to the northwest and move "like a swarm," darting in random directions and changing course. At times they flare very bright and turn red or orange, then dim out again. Sometimes they seem far away, and sometimes they seem close to what the witness called the juniper mountains near the dunes. The last time, the witness counted about 10 orbs at once.

Two details stand out. Each orb had a haze or aura around it, and there were no blinking lights, the kind you would expect from drones or aircraft. The witness put the duration at about two hours.

NUFORC logged it as report 201418 and posted it October 12, and Idaho radio station KEZJ picked up the story on October 15. No agency has offered an explanation. It is a single witness, the date and time are listed as approximate, and no photo or video is attached, so drones, flares or satellites can't be ruled out. But if you live near St. Anthony, the report says the show starts around 10 p.m., off to the northwest.

Wilder, Kentucky. Bobby Mackey's Music World, 1978.

For decades, country singer Bobby Mackey's honky tonk in Wilder, Kentucky, was promoted as "the most haunted nightclub in America." Mackey bought the property in 1978, and he has said the site was a slaughterhouse before a roadhouse went up there, one that ran under several names, including The Brisbane.

The legends grew from there. Local legends call the place a "gateway to hell," complete with a claimed "portal to hell" and a basement wall whose water stains are said to look like human faces. The legends say several spirits haunt it, including Pearl Bryan, a 22-year-old pregnant Sunday school teacher from Greencastle, Indiana, whose headless body was found in 1896 about two and a half miles away in Fort Thomas, Kentucky. Two dental students were convicted of her murder and hanged in 1897, but one legend claims her killers were Satanists who cursed the site. Another tells of a pregnant dancer named Johanna who is said to have taken her own life in the 1940s after her father murdered her lover, a singer at the club. Mackey, his wife Janet and caretaker Carl Lawson appeared on Jerry Springer in 1991 and Geraldo in 1992, and Ghost Adventures featured the club in its premiere episode in 2008.

Then come the skeptics. Searches of property records, newspapers and court files found no evidence for the legends, and no link has ever been established between the club and Pearl Bryan's murder. Science writer Sharon A. Hill called the supernatural claims and the "portal to hell" unsubstantiated, noting that the stories picked up new details over decades of retelling. The Campbell County Historical and Genealogical Society says it is "highly unlikely" that Pearl Bryan's ghost haunts the place, and a Northern Kentucky Tribune reporter who took the two-hour tour twice wrote that nothing happened to suggest it was haunted.

In March 2024 the club closed, with plans to move temporarily to Florence, Kentucky, while a new building goes up on the old site, and the owners said the "portal" and the face-stained basement wall would be relocated too. The original building was demolished on December 10, 2024. Whatever was in that basement, it is apparently moving with the band.

Savannah, Georgia. 6 West Harris Street, March 1860.

On Madison Square in Savannah stands the Sorrel-Weed House, a Greek Revival mansion designed by architect Charles Cluskey for shipping merchant Francis Sorrel. In 1954 it became one of the first two homes in Georgia named a State Landmark, Robert E. Lee visited the family there, and the floating-feather opening of Forrest Gump was filmed from its rooftop. It is also billed as one of the most haunted buildings in Savannah, with ghost tours inside every evening.

The story told on many of those tours goes like this. Francis Sorrel carried on an affair with a young enslaved woman named Molly, kept in quarters above the carriage house. His wife, Matilda, discovered them and leapt from the balcony to her death in the courtyard, and a few weeks later, the tale says, Molly was found hanged in the carriage house. Visitors describe sudden nausea and a choking feeling in the basement, panic for no reason, and fully charged phone and camera batteries that are dead by the end of the tour. Ghost Hunters, Ghost Adventures and BuzzFeed Unsolved have all investigated the house.

Historians tell a different story. Francis Sorrel sold the house to Henry D. Weed on June 14, 1859, and moved his family next door to 12 West Harris Street. Matilda died on March 27, 1860, and a letter written that same day by family friend Charles C. Jones Jr. says she sprang from a window of her residence on Harris Street, "next door to the house which was the family mansion for so many years." No Sorrel family record mentions an enslaved woman named Molly, and an archaeological dig showed that a depression in the carriage house floor, rumored to be a grave, was really an old trash pit. Historians point out that even as fiction, the Molly tale reflects the very real abuse enslaved women suffered in that era.

So if something really does walk these halls, who is it? Savannah ghost author James Caskey has floated another answer: the house sits on or near the southern tip of the British earthworks from the 1779 Siege of Savannah, which many historians call the bloodiest hour of the entire American Revolution.

Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sorrel-Weed_House

Have you ever wondered what the Star of Bethlehem really was?

Top 5 things to know about the star the wise men followed:

1) In the Gospel of Matthew, chapter 2, wise men from the East follow a star to Jerusalem, where King Herod's chief priests and scribes point them to Bethlehem in Judea, south of Jerusalem, and the star goes before them until it stops over the place where the child Jesus was.

2) Matthew is the only one of the four Gospels to mention the star or the Magi, and the Greek word magi there probably means astronomers or astrologers, which was awkward for an early Church that condemned astrology.

3) In 1614 German astronomer Johannes Kepler worked out that Jupiter and Saturn met in a series of three conjunctions in 7 BC, though modern calculations show the two planets stayed nearly a degree apart, so it would not have been much of a show.

4) Other theories include a strikingly close Jupiter and Venus conjunction on June 17, 2 BC, a comet or nova that Chinese and Korean stargazers watched for over seventy days around 5 BC, and astronomer Michael Molnar's double occultation of Jupiter by the Moon on April 17, 6 BC, which scientists, theologians and historians debated at the University of Groningen in October 2014.

5) Many Christians believe the star was a miraculous sign, and John Chrysostom asked how a star could point out a spot as small as a manger unless it "came down, and stood over the very head of the young child," while some modern scholars see the story as a pious fiction.

Top 5 things to know about the night something splashed down off Nova Scotia:

Have you heard of the Mogollon Monster?

Top 5 things to know about the creature some call the Arizona Bigfoot:

1) The Mogollon Monster is said to roam central and eastern Arizona along the Mogollon Rim, and cryptozoologist Don Davis claimed he saw it in the mid-1940s on a Boy Scout trip near Payson, Arizona, describing a huge creature with a square, box-like head and massive arms.

2) It's usually described as an ape-like creature over 7 feet tall with large red eyes, long black or reddish-brown hair, and a smell compared to "dead fish, a skunk with bad body odor, decaying peat moss and the musk of a snapping turtle."

3) Reports say it walks with wide strides, leaves footprints about 22 inches long, mimics birds and coyotes, whistles, throws stones from hiding, builds nests of pine needles and twigs, and lets out a scream like a woman in "great distress."

4) The oldest known report ran in The Arizona Republican in 1903, when I.W. Stevens described a creature near the Grand Canyon with long white hair, a matted beard down to its knees and claws at least two inches long, and said it threatened him with a club.

5) Northern Arizona University biology professor emeritus Stan Lindstedt puts it "in the category of mythology," and scientists point to hoaxes or misidentified black bears, mountain lions and elk, noting that grizzly bears still roamed Arizona's forests as recently as the early 1930s.

Answer: B) Snallygaster

The Snallygaster is said to haunt Frederick County, Maryland, especially South Mountain, Braddock Heights and the Middletown Valley. Its roots go back to the German immigrants who settled the area beginning in the 1730s and told of a monster called a Schneller Geist, meaning "quick ghost." Legend describes it as half bird and half reptile, with a metallic beak lined with razor-sharp teeth and octopus-like tentacles, swooping silently out of the sky to carry off its victims. Seven-pointed stars, said to keep it away, can still be seen painted on local barns. In February and March 1909, newspapers reported a beast with "enormous wings, a long pointed bill, claws like steel hooks, and an eye in the center of its forehead" that screeched "like a locomotive whistle." The Smithsonian Institution reportedly offered a reward for its hide, and President Theodore Roosevelt reportedly considered postponing an African safari to hunt it himself. It later came out that the 1909 reports were a hoax by Middletown Valley Register editor George C. Rhoderick and reporter Ralph S. Wolfe to sell more papers. In 2021, the American Snallygaster Museum opened in Libertytown, Maryland.

Near Keene, North Dakota. October 7, 2026, about 10:55 p.m.

An oil production worker was on night shift, checking on well sites spread out between New Town and Mandaree, the same rounds as every other night. Around 10:55 he pulled onto a well pad and noticed two lights over the next hill, stacked one on top of the other, sitting low, close together and perfectly still above the grassland.

At first he figured it was a new communications tower. But his company's towers carry blue and red lights, and he hadn't seen any new construction out there. Something felt off, so he started recording.

The moment he stopped and reached for his binoculars, the top light started speeding off in his direction, gaining altitude, and a few seconds later it went dark. The lower light held still for another 30 seconds or so, then it sped off and went dark too.

About a minute passed with nothing to see. Then he heard a humming, almost like a vibration. He got out of his vehicle, looked around, and saw a triangle with three lights moving slowly, directly over top of him. No red or green position lights, no flashing beacons, just three solid lights. He recorded again, and when he stopped and looked back up, he could never find it again.

He drove as far as he could on company property toward where the lights had been hovering. He found nothing out of the ordinary, except that the cattle in the pasture were wound up and lively for that time of night. He says he checked FlightRadar, and there were no planes or other aircraft anywhere close.

He filed his report with the National UFO Reporting Center the next day, describing a black triangle listed at 30 by 30 in size, with a haze around it, moving at an estimated 50 to 150 miles per hour. He says he recorded video both times. It's a single witness, and NUFORC hasn't attached any explanation. Drones would be the first ordinary suspect, but the slow pass right overhead, the hum and the missing position lights are the details he made a point of reporting.

New Orleans Square, Disneyland, Anaheim, California. Photographed in 1968, posted August 2026.

Tom Eubank, 84, only wanted to sell his old Canon camera. He'd gotten it in 1963 while serving aboard a Navy ship in the Mediterranean. His granddaughter, Josie Weaver, was helping, and to see what was still on the old film, the two of them tracked down a projector.

Up on the screen came his 1968 trip to Disneyland: the train station, the Swiss Family Treehouse, it's a small world, Pirates of the Caribbean and Sleeping Beauty Castle. And in one shot of New Orleans Square, front and center, stood a man who didn't seem to belong there.

He's wearing a navy blue crewneck T-shirt and modern-looking sunglasses, with a haircut faded on the sides and a square case on a strap over his shoulder, while the guests around him are dressed more formally, in brighter colors. "He looked so different to everyone around him, especially with his haircut," Weaver told People. "It just looked like someone that we would see out and about now."

She posted it to TikTok on August 25 with the caption "found a time traveler in my grandpas film," and it took off, with millions of views and more than a thousand comments. "Bro is from 2010," one wrote. Her grandfather agreed the man looked out of place, but when she suggested a time traveler, he just laughed. Her grandmother was blunter: "These are just old photos."

Plenty of commenters side with Grandma. Sunglasses like his were already around, T-shirts as outerwear had been popular since the 1940s, and one said the case is just a camera bag of the era. Even Weaver hedged in her own caption, noting that Ray-Ban dates back to the 1930s. To this day, nobody has identified the man in the frame.

Newburgh Brewing Company, South Colden Street, Newburgh, New York. October 2026.

The brewery sits in a building that dates to the 1850s. Before the beer, it housed a steam engine operation, a yarn factory and the Newburgh Paper Box Company. In February 2024, owner Paul Halayko put a motion-activated security camera in the kitchen, and it started picking up things he can't explain.

In one frame, a white shape seems to turn into a face. "Kind of like a grimaced mouth right here," he told News 12. "Very creepy with the teeth, definitely see two eyes." Two other overnight recordings caught flashes of light about 47 minutes apart while nobody was inside. Side-by-side stills show pots, a garbage pail, a tray and knives that seem to have moved or vanished. "We've got two knives right there in the middle on the knife rack," he said. "Now let's go to the next photo, they are gone." A worker has also reported seeing a man in overalls several times downstairs in the production area, and describes those encounters as positive.

Halayko asked the city historian whether anyone had ever died in the building. She found no recorded fatal accident, though she warned that industrial work was dangerous and some deaths may never have been written down.

Then, after News 12's first report aired, historian Salvatore LaBruna turned up a New York Times article from January 20, 1867. Two days earlier, a boiler at the Washington Iron Works, an early ironworks tied to the brewery's historic property, blew apart and tore through a brick wall. A 45-year-old worker named Hugh Elwood was thrown against a wall and pinned under the wreckage. Rescuers worked for about an hour to free him, and he died as he was carried out, leaving a wife and four children. A coroner's jury blamed a defective boiler and poor safety precautions. Co-owner Chris Basso says the owners had no idea.

None of the recordings actually show anything moving, and bugs or dust drifting past a motion camera would be the first suspects. Halayko isn't ruling anything out. "I'd be crazy to say it's not possible," he said, "because there are many things in this world that we don't understand."

Ellsworth Air Force Base missile field, near Newell, South Dakota. November 1977.

Mario Woods was a young Air Force security policeman with the 44th Missile Security Squadron, guarding Minuteman II nuclear missiles buried under the western South Dakota prairie. One night in November 1977, he said, he and his partner Michael Johnson answered an alarm at a launch facility called November-5.

Woods said an enormous glowing object was waiting near the site. Intense light came down over their truck, they could barely move, and a smaller dark sphere hung near the vehicle. Then figures approached. The next thing he knew, he was coming to beside a reservoir near Newell, miles away, with hours of his life unaccounted for. Afterward, he said, the two men were separated, questioned and examined, and they lost touch for decades.

He spent most of the next 49 years looking for Johnson. In June 2026 they finally reconnected by phone, and on September 7 the YouTube program American Alchemy published their reunion. Johnson's own waking memories overlap with Woods' on a huge, close light, being unable to move, and a confused aftermath.

On October 16, 2026, just weeks after that reunion, Mario Woods died of leukemia. He was 71.

The debate around his story is real. The missile field, the squadron and the two-man alarm teams all check out, but no duty roster, alarm log or medical record from that night has been published. Much of the detail about beings and procedures surfaced under hypnosis, and the Justice Department warns that memories recovered that way can't be assumed accurate. Even the date gets garbled online: November-5 is the name of the launch site, not the day, and Woods placed the night around November 18. And the best-known 1977 Ellsworth UFO document, a different story entirely, was exposed as a hoax back in 1984.

Whatever happened out there, he carried it for half a century, and he found the one man who could share it with weeks to spare.

Near Rocky Arbor State Park, Wisconsin Dells, Wisconsin. Reported October 5, 2026.

A driver was heading toward Wisconsin Dells to pick up an Applebee's order, top down on what they believe was a late-90s Chrysler Sebring convertible. It was the end of sunset, and they figured it would be a pretty ride. By the time they reached the stretch of highway that runs past Rocky Arbor State Park, a small park just outside the resort town, it was darker than they expected.

On the side of the road that isn't open to the public, there's a dirt road entrance where the driver says they've seen police park from time to time. That's where something was standing. "But standing there clear as day was a large creature 9-12 feet I'm guessing," they wrote on Reddit, "with legs that looked like the back legs of a dog but a huge chest and arms like a human and a dogs face with bright yellow eyes."

Eureka Springs, Arkansas. 75 Prospect Avenue, 1937.

The Crescent Hotel opened in 1886 high above Eureka Springs as a resort for wealthy travelers, designed by architect Isaac S. Taylor and fitted with luxuries like electricity and elevators. It never quite thrived as a hotel. From 1908 to 1934 it housed the Crescent College and Conservatory for Young Women, and after that it went back to being a summer hotel.

Then, in 1937, Norman G. Baker bought it. Baker was a millionaire inventor and radio personality from Iowa with no medical training, and he had already been run out of Iowa after the state won an injunction against him for practicing medicine without a license. He turned the Crescent into a hospital and health resort, decorated the interior in his trademark shades of purple, and claimed to have a cure for cancer. Postal inspectors claimed it cleared about 500,000 dollars in one year. In January 1940 a federal court in his mail fraud case called the cure a "pure hoax" and "utterly false." He was sentenced to four years and served his time at Leavenworth from 1941 to 1944. The hotel closed while he was in prison.

That history is the real horror, and it is where most of the ghost stories come from. The hotel now calls itself America's Most Haunted Hotel. Room 218 is tied to Michael, a stonemason said to have died during construction. Room 419 is known as Theodora's room, where staff say a Baker patient who also worked as a hospital assistant keeps turning up. Guests and staff tell of a nurse pushing a gurney down a third floor hall before she vanishes, and of children seen under the autopsy table in the old morgue, which is now a stop on the nightly tour. In 2005 the Ghost Hunters team said their thermal camera caught a full-body apparition.

In 2019, an archaeological dig on the grounds turned up more than 500 bottles from the Baker years, and the hotel says some held his "cures" and others held specimens taken from patients. The fraud is documented fact. Whether anyone still walks those halls is the part people argue about.

Coronado, California. Hotel del Coronado, November 1892.

On November 24, 1892, a young woman checks into the Hotel del Coronado alone and signs the register as "Mrs. Lottie A. Bernard, Detroit." Staff later describe her as ladylike, beautiful, reserved and well dressed, but troubled and melancholy. On November 29 she is found dead on an exterior staircase leading down to the beach, with a gunshot wound to the head.

Her real name was Kate Morgan. Born Kate Farmer in Iowa around 1864, she lost her mother as a small child, married Thomas Morgan in 1885, and lost their baby son when he was just two days old. Around 1890 she ran off with Albert Allen, a relative by marriage. When she arrived at the Del, she was alone and ill. The San Diego County coroner determined the wound was self-inflicted, and she was buried at nearby Mount Hope Cemetery.

That is where the arguments start. In the 1980s, San Francisco lawyer Alan May suggested foul play, pointing to a passing statement at the coroner's inquest that the bullet that killed her did not match her gun. The hotel's own historian later wrote a book about her, The Beautiful Stranger, drawing on libraries, historical societies, city hall and police files, and it leans toward the official verdict of suicide. Neither side has ever settled it.

Meanwhile, locals say Kate Morgan never checked out. Room 502, where she stayed, is now the most requested room in the hotel, and the Del runs weekend ghost tours called Haunted Happenings. Suicide, murder, or a guest who simply won't leave? People keep asking for her room.

The Mounds Theatre opened in 1922 in the Dayton's Bluff neighborhood on St. Paul's East Side, billed as "The Pride of Dayton's Bluff," with silent movies and live entertainment. Green Swamp, near Lakeland, Florida. The night of February 8, 2026.

A Sasquatch researcher identified only as BD heads out alone from a campground in a wildlife management area in the Green Swamp, in Polk County. He is experienced but skeptical, an Army combat veteran who has spent years researching this swamp. It is a clear night and a cold one. He waits half an hour to let his eyes adjust, then creeps down the trail in near-total darkness, scanning ahead with a night vision camera and taking only 10 to 15 steps at a time.

About a tenth of a mile in, the eyes of a deer shine back at him. Then comes a whistle from his left, maybe 30 to 40 meters away near a cypress swamp, short and sharp like the "white" in a bobwhite quail's call, a sound that feels out of place that late at night. He remembers his grandmother telling him never to whistle in the woods. He keeps walking, and something starts moving in the brush behind him, always staying about 25 meters back. Then a second whistle.

Most of a mile in, a third whistle comes, and without thinking he whistles back. He says he instantly regretted it. One whistle answers from his left, then another from his right. Now there are two of them, and they start leapfrogging: one moves up and whistles, then the other passes it and does the same, staying within about 50 meters of each other and never getting ahead of him. He calls it tactical, like military units tracking a target.

At the next trail intersection he turns, crawls into a pocket of scrub, lies in a shallow hollow and pulls his hoodie over his head, breathing into his sleeve. He listens as something moves through the area in what he describes as a systematic search for 15 to 20 minutes before retreating. He stays hidden about 90 minutes, then hurries back to camp.

He never saw what was out there, and the North American Wood Ape Conservancy files this one as a vocalization report, not a sighting. Other hikers, deer or night birds would be the first explanations, but BD knows this swamp's wildlife and the other researchers who use it extremely well. When investigator Tami Grimes walked the route with him six days later, the night brought owls, a call like "a hound with laryngitis," a loud percussive sound from the cypress bog, and a piece of wood that landed at his feet. Monroe, Louisiana. October 2026.

Out in the Ouachita River floodplain near Monroe sits Watson Brake, eleven earthen mounds from 3 to 25 feet tall, joined by ridges into an oval nearly 900 feet across. Radiocarbon dates published in the journal Science in 1997 put the start of mound building around 3500 B.C. That makes it the oldest earthwork mound complex in North America, older than Egypt's pyramids and older than Stonehenge. Most of the site is still privately owned, and it is not open to the public.

This month Charisma Magazine asked whether the mounds could hide a biblical secret. The article walks through the work of author L.A. Marzulli and his series On the Trail of the Nephilim. Marzulli reads Genesis 6 as describing giants born to fallen angels and human women, and he proposes that some Nephilim tribes escaped Canaan during its conquest and migrated to other parts of the world, an idea that drives his search for traces of them in the Americas. He points to old newspaper accounts of skeletons 12 feet tall or more, to archival photos from Catalina Island that four analysts he cites estimated at about 9 feet, and to the precise geometry of Ohio's Newark Earthworks. At Poverty Point, a younger mound site in Louisiana, his team timed a laborer digging with a replica flint hoe and calculated that the enormous mound there would have taken about 26 million bucketloads of earth. "Something is wrong with this picture!" he wrote. He calls the mounds "the fingerprints of the supernatural."

Archaeologists tell a very different story. The team that dated Watson Brake says it was built in stages by seasonal hunter-gatherers who lived on fish, shellfish and river animals, used local stone and gravel for their tools and cooking, and abandoned the site around 2800 B.C. Those builders helped overturn old assumptions about who could organize monumental construction. Still, even the archaeologist quoted in the Charisma piece admits it is unclear why Watson Brake and the other mounds of its age were built. Patient people with a plan, or something bigger? The ground near Monroe isn't saying.

Valley of Elah, ancient Israel. 1 Samuel 17.

In 1 Samuel 17, the Israelites under Saul face the Philistines in the Valley of Elah. Twice a day for 40 days, morning and evening, Goliath of Gath, the Philistine champion, steps out between the lines and challenges Israel to send a man to fight him in single combat. Saul is afraid. The young shepherd David takes only his staff, his sling and five stones from a brook, hits Goliath in the forehead, and cuts off his head with the giant's own sword.

Here is where it gets blurry. The Masoretic Text, the basis of most Bibles, gives Goliath's height as six cubits and a span, about 9 feet 9 inches. But the Dead Sea Scrolls text of Samuel from the late 1st century BC, the 1st century historian Josephus and the Greek Septuagint all say four cubits and a span, about 6 feet 9 inches. Many scholars think the smaller number grew as the text was copied, possibly when a scribe's eye was drawn to the number six a verse later. The Septuagint also tells a significantly shorter version of the whole story.

Then there is 2 Samuel 21:19, which says Goliath the Gittite was killed by Elhanan, a Bethlehemite. 1 Chronicles 20:5 later says Elhanan killed Lahmi, Goliath's brother, which most scholars dismiss as an obvious harmonization. The scholarly consensus is that the Elhanan account is the older text, and that the author of 1 Samuel folded Goliath into David's story. Archaeology adds one more twist: at Tell es-Safi, biblical Gath, excavators found a potsherd dated to the 10th to mid-9th centuries BC inscribed with two names etymologically related to Goliath.

Weston, West Virginia. Trans-Allegheny Lunatic Asylum, opened to patients in October 1864.

Virginia authorized the asylum in 1858, and construction began with prison labor and blue sandstone quarried at nearby Mount Clare. The Civil War interrupted the work, and the 7th Ohio Volunteer Infantry seized the unused building fund from a local bank and delivered it to Wheeling, where it became a start-up treasury for what would become the new state of West Virginia. Designed by Richard Snowden Andrews on the Kirkbride Plan, the main building is said to be one of the largest hand-cut stone buildings in the United States, and it is a National Historic Landmark.

It was built for 250 patients. It held 717 by 1880 and about 2,600 at its peak in the 1950s. People were admitted for reasons that included asthma, laziness, egotism, domestic troubles and greediness. A 1949 Charleston Gazette series found poor sanitation and too little furniture, lighting and heat. Patients underwent insulin shock, electroshock, hydrotherapy and lobotomies, and in the early 1950s the hospital was home to the West Virginia Lobotomy Project with Walter Freeman. There is no official count of the patients who died there; research is underway, and estimates could reach five figures. It closed in May 1994.

That is the documented part. The legend took over after Morgantown contractor Joe Jordan bought the 242,000-square-foot building at a 2007 auction for 1.5 million dollars. Since 2008 it has offered historic tours, paranormal tours, overnight ghost hunts and an autumn haunted house, with guides dressed as 19th-century nurses. Ghost Hunters, Ghost Adventures, Paranormal Lockdown and Portals to Hell have all featured it as a haunted location.

Japan. Jōren Falls, Izu, Shizuoka Prefecture.

The jorōgumo is a yōkai, a creature of Japanese folklore: a spider that can shapeshift into a beautiful woman. It appears in Edo period writings such as the Taihei-Hyakumonogatari and the Tonoigusa. In one Tonoigusa tale, a young woman carrying a child approaches a warrior and tells the child to go and be embraced by its father. He sees through the ploy, strikes her with his sword, and she flees to the attic. The next day a dead jorōgumo one or two shaku long is found there, along with the bodies of people it had devoured. Artist Toriyama Sekien pictured it as a spider woman controlling small fire-breathing spiders.

At the Jōren Falls of Izu, legend says a man resting beside the basin felt webs thrown around his leg. He moved the silk onto a tree stump, and the stump was dragged into the falls instead. Later a woodcutter dropped his axe in the basin, and a beautiful woman returned it, telling him never to tell anyone what he saw. Days later, drunk at a banquet, he told the whole story, went to sleep, and never woke. In Sendai, the same stump legend explains the name Kashikobuchi, the "clever abyss," where a voice was heard saying "clever, clever" after the stump was pulled under. That jorōgumo was worshipped for warding off water disasters, and monuments and torii there still bear its name.

That is the legend. The documented creature is smaller. Japanese entomologists use the name jorōgumo for the spider Trichonephila clavata, which English speakers now call the Joro spider. The yōkai lives on in Demon Slayer's Spider Demon mother, Monster Hunter Rise and other modern stories.

Long Beach, California. RMS Queen Mary, moored at the Port of Long Beach since 1967.

The Queen Mary sailed on her maiden voyage for the Cunard Line on May 27, 1936, and won the Blue Riband for speed that August. In World War II she was painted navy gray and converted into a troopship, often carrying as many as 15,000 men in a single voyage, and her new color and her speed earned her the nickname the Grey Ghost. On October 2, 1942, she accidentally sliced through one of her own escorts, the light cruiser HMS Curacoa, off the Irish coast, with a loss of 338 lives. Under orders not to stop because of the U-boat risk, she steamed on with a fractured stem.

Cunard retired her in 1967. The City of Long Beach bought her, she left Southampton for the last time on October 31, 1967, and she opened to tourists as a hotel and museum in 1971.

That is the documented part. Here is where the legend starts. Claims that the ship was haunted began in earnest in the 1980s, possibly started by employees to increase business or spook guests, and they have grown since. In 2008 Time magazine put her on its Top 10 Haunted Places list. The stories include a stateroom haunted by a person supposedly murdered there, a young girl who haunts the former second class pool, and a father who murdered his two daughters on board. But there is no historical record that anyone was murdered aboard, and most deaths on the ship were from natural causes. Joe Nickell of the Center for Inquiry blames pareidolia and the daydreaming common among workers doing repetitive chores.

Philippines. Capiz province, Panay Island, Western Visayas.

Aswang is a catch-all word in Filipino folklore for evil shape-shifting creatures: vampires, ghouls, witches, viscera suckers and human-beast hybrids that turn into dogs, cats or pigs. Spanish colonists made the first written records of it in the 16th century and noted it was the most feared of all the islands' monsters. Folklorist Maximo Ramos sorted the aswang into five types: the vampire, the self-segmenting viscera sucker, the weredog, the witch and the ghoul. In the stories, an aswang lives quietly among villagers by day, sometimes by marrying into the community, and hunts at night.

The protection lore is everywhere. Wakes were kept brightly lit so an aswang could not steal the corpse. Salt, ash, vinegar, holy objects and the tail of a stingray were said to drive one off, sharp sticks or bolos were pushed between the bamboo floor slats, and a special coconut oil hung at the door was said to boil when an aswang came near. One test: if your reflection in someone's eye is upside down, you are looking at an aswang.

That is the legend. Here is the documented part. Capiz is so tied to the creature that it is called its hometown. Anthropologists point to two likely sparks: the "tiktik" and "wakwak" calls of bats and Philippine flying lemurs, and X-linked dystonia parkinsonism, a genetic disorder concentrated on Panay whose twisting symptoms led sufferers to be branded aswang and shunned. And during the Huk Rebellion of the early 1950s, the CIA spread rumors that evil men would be attacked by an aswang, then punctured a dead Huk fighter's body, drained its blood and left it on a road. Colonel Edward Lansdale was likely among those who spread the story.

Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. Eastern State Penitentiary, opened October 25, 1829.

When Eastern State opened in the Fairmount section of Philadelphia, it was the largest and most expensive public building ever erected in the United States. Architect John Haviland laid out its cellblocks like the spokes of a wagon wheel around a central hub. Each prisoner lived alone in a cell lit by one skylight, called the Eye of God, and whenever a man left his cell, a guard put a hood over his head so he could not see or be seen. The idea, known as the Pennsylvania system, was that silence and solitude would make criminals truly penitent. More than 300 prisons copied the design.

That is where the controversy starts. Charles Dickens visited in 1842 and wrote, "I hold this slow, and daily, tampering with the mysteries of the brain to be immeasurably worse than any torture of the body." Guards also used cold showers, the iron gag and a restraint chair, and the punishment cells beneath Cellblock 14 were known as the Hole. Overcrowding finally broke the system, and solitary confinement was abandoned in 1913.

The famous inmates come with their own debate. Al Capone served time there in 1929 on a stretch of cells nicknamed Park Avenue, and newspapers reported he lived in luxury. The museum now says those stories may have been exaggerated, since one document says he bought his fancy radio from the cell's previous occupant and another mentions a cellmate. In 1945 Willie Sutton and eleven others escaped through a 97-foot tunnel.

The prison closed in 1971, and trees grew inside the cellblocks before it opened for tours in 1994. Some visitors say they have "sensed something." The museum's own audio tour tells of shadowy figures darting from cell to cell, and of a locksmith who felt what he called an incredible and powerful energy while removing a 142-year-old lock from an abandoned cell. Ghost Hunters and Ghost Adventures have both filmed there. As the tour puts it, the building is certainly haunting, if not haunted.

New Orleans, Louisiana. 1140 Royal Street, April 10, 1834.

Delphine LaLaurie is one of the best known socialites in New Orleans. In 1831 she bought property on Royal Street in the French Quarter, and by 1832 a mansion with attached slave quarters stood there. Rumors about how she treated the people she enslaved had already spread through the city. Funeral registers record the deaths of 12 enslaved people at the house between 1830 and 1834, with no causes listed.

On April 10, 1834, a fire breaks out in the kitchen. Responders find the 70-year-old cook chained to the stove. She later says she set the fire because she feared punishment, and that people taken to the uppermost room never came back. When the LaLauries refuse to hand over the keys, bystanders break down the doors and find seven enslaved people who had been imprisoned and abused for months. A mob sacks the mansion until there is scarcely anything left but the walls. LaLaurie escapes by coach and schooner to Mobile, Alabama, then to Paris. She is never brought to justice, and she dies in Paris in 1849.

That is the documented part. Here is where the debate starts. The building tourists photograph today is not the house she lived in. Hers was burned and left in ruins for at least four years, then rebuilt after 1838 by Pierre Trastour. And many of the most horrifying details told on tours do not come from 1834. Writer Jeanne DeLavigne added explicit tortures in her 1946 book Ghost Stories of Old New Orleans without citing sources, a ghost tour operator added more in 1998, and neither set of claims is supported by the primary sources. Some modern retellings put the death toll as high as 100.

None of that has slowed the legend. It is commonly called the Haunted House. Nicolas Cage bought it in 2007 for 3.45 million dollars and lost it to foreclosure in 2009, and Kathy Bates won an Emmy playing LaLaurie in American Horror Story. The cruelty is real history. The ghosts are still argued over.

Top 5 things to know about the legendary cup of the Last Supper:

1) In Valencia, Spain, the cathedral keeps the Holy Chalice, an agate cup that is one of only two surviving relics tied to the Grail, and while its bowl may date to Greco-Roman times, nothing is known about it before 1399, when it was gifted to King Martin I of Aragon.

2) The Grail first appears around 1190 in Perceval, the Story of the Grail, an unfinished romance by Chrétien de Troyes, where it is a mysterious serving dish that is wondrous but not clearly holy.

3) Soon after, Robert de Boron made it the vessel Jesus used at the Last Supper, which Joseph of Arimathea used to catch Christ's blood at the crucifixion, while other writers made it a stone or a treasure guarded by the Fisher King in a hidden castle.

4) The other survivor, the green Sacro Catino in Genoa, Italy, was long thought to be carved from emerald, until it was broken during Napoleon's conquest and turned out to be glass.

5) Glastonbury, England, claims Joseph of Arimathea founded its abbey, and in 1906 a group including Wellesley Tudor Pole retrieved a glass bowl that John Goodchild had hidden nearby and promoted it as the original Holy Grail.

Have you heard of the Kenneth Arnold sighting?

Top 5 things to know about the sighting that gave us the flying saucer:

1) On June 24, 1947, private pilot Kenneth Arnold was flying near Mineral, Washington, at about 9,200 feet, after detouring to search for a crashed Marine Corps C-46 that carried a 5,000 dollar reward.

2) A few minutes before 3 p.m. he saw a bright flash, then nine shiny objects flying in a long chain past Mount Rainier, weaving like the tail of a Chinese kite and flipping on their edges in mirror-like flashes.

3) He timed them from Mount Rainier to Mount Adams, about 50 miles, in one minute and 42 seconds, which worked out to over 1,700 miles per hour, and he rounded it down to 1,200, still faster than any known aircraft of the day.

4) When reporters interviewed him in Pendleton, Oregon, he compared the objects to a saucer, a disc and a pie pan, the press quickly coined the terms flying saucer and flying disc, and it became the first postwar sighting in the U.S. to make nationwide news.

5) The Army Air Forces publicly blamed a mirage, skeptics later suggested meteors or American white pelicans, and Arnold told the Associated Press, "Half the people look at me as a combination of Einstein, Flash Gordon and screwball."

Have you heard of Resurrection Mary?

Top 5 things to know about Chicago's most famous ghost:

1) Her story centers on Resurrection Cemetery in Justice, Illinois, a few miles southwest of Chicago, where since the 1930s drivers on Archer Avenue have reported picking up a young woman who vanishes as they near the cemetery.

2) She is described as a blonde with blue eyes in a white party dress, sometimes with a thin shawl, dancing shoes and a small clutch purse, and she usually says very little on the ride.

3) The legend says Mary left a dance at the Oh Henry Ballroom after an argument with her boyfriend, was killed walking up Archer Avenue by a hit and run driver who was never found, and was buried at Resurrection in her white dress.

4) In 1939 Jerry Palus said he danced with her and even kissed her, then drove her home along Archer Avenue, where she got out in front of the cemetery and disappeared, and a 1979 newspaper column told of a cab driver who swore she vanished from his car without the door ever opening.

5) In August 1976 she supposedly left burned handprints on the cemetery's iron fence, though officials said a truck damaged it, and researchers still argue over whether she was Mary Bregovy, who died in 1934, or 12-year-old Anna "Marija" Norkus, who died in 1927.
